problem: The line is corrupted and unreadable: 'DC gain z1/p1 1p1).' A student cannot tell whether the lead bracket DC gain is above or below 1, and the missing inequality is the whole point of the lead/lag distinction.
fix: Lead bracket: DC gain z1/p1 < 1, because p1 > z1; the gain rises towards 1 as frequency goes high. (Contrast: lag bracket DC gain z2/p2 > 1, falling to 1 at high frequency.)

problem: Two different bullets make two different parameters responsible for the same steady-state-error gain: β is found from the error specification and the lag pole is set to ωz2/β (so the lag alone gives a low-frequency boost of β), yet the next bullet says to raise Kc so the low-frequency gain meets the error constant. A student who does both gets a low-frequency gain β times too large.
fix: Say clearly which parameter carries the error constant. For example: 'The lag supplies the low-frequency boost β; Kc only scales the whole compensator, so choose Kc = (required error-constant gain)/(plant DC gain × β).' Or, if Kc is set from the error constant first, then β is chosen only to bring the gain at the new crossover back to 0 dB.

problem: 's = jω is the Laplace variable in rad/s' is loose: s is the complex Laplace variable, and only on the frequency-response plot is it restricted to s = jω.
fix: s is the Laplace variable; on the Bode plot s = jω, with ω the frequency in rad/s.

problem: The formula writes the lead bracket first, while the figure and its caption put the lag section first. Multiplication is commutative, so nothing is wrong mathematically, but the mismatch can make a student think the two orderings mean different compensators.
fix: Add one line: 'The order of the two brackets does not matter; the product is the same. The block diagram shows lag first only by convention.' Or write the formula with the lag bracket first to match the figure.
